title: Impact of Plasmonic Modes and Thermophysical Properties on the Double-Pulse Structuring of Highly-Ordered LIPSS for Biosensing Applications
authors: G. D. Tsibidis, F. Fraggelakis, P. Lingos, E. Cusworth, V. G. Kravets, A. N. Grigorenko, A. V. Kabashin, E. Stratakis
abstract: The fabrication of highly ordered laser-induced periodic surface structures (LIPSS) on thin metallic films is dictated, predomaninatly, by a synergy of periodic electromagnetic energy deposition and complex fluid dynamics. In this work, we present a combined experimental and theoretical study on the formation of ultra-regular LIPSS on 32-nm-thick Au films using a double-pulse femtosecond laser scheme. We demonstrate that for thin films, the excitation of coupled Surface Plasmon Polaritons (SPPs) at both interfaces dictates the initial energy distribution. On the othe hand, the final morphology is greatly influenced by hydrodynamical processes. Interestingly, due to the low electron-phonon coupling of Au and the high thermal confinement of the thin film, single-pulse irradiation leads to uncontrolled hydrodynamic instabilities a non uniform topographies. Thus, we demonstrate that a double-pulse approach with an optimized interpulse delay (Δτ=1.2 ns) effectively controls the melt duration and viscosity, suppressing complex fluid motion and promoting the growth of highly ordered arrays. These structures support narrow surface lattice resonances (SLRs) suitable for high-sensitivity plasmonic biosensing.
summary: This work details the controlled fabrication of highly-ordered plasmonic nanostructures on thin gold films using a double-pulse femtosecond laser approach. By managing the transient fluid dynamics through optimized pulse timing, the researchers suppress chaotic melting and achieve structures exhibiting narrow Surface Lattice Resonances. These highly ordered plasmonic arrays are presented as a robust platform for next-generation, ultrasensitive biosensing.
main_problem: The primary goal is to fabricate highly-ordered Laser-Induced Periodic Surface Structures (LIPSS) on thin metallic films for use in high-sensitivity plasmonic biosensing.
main_result: The use of a double-pulse femtosecond laser scheme, optimized with a specific interpulse delay, successfully controls the fluid dynamics, leading to highly-uniform LIPSS that exhibit narrow Surface Lattice Resonances (SLRs).
method: The study combines experimental techniques (femtosecond laser processing, SEM, ellipsometry) with theoretical modeling (3D-FDTD, Two-Temperature Model, Navier-Stokes equations).
model_or_system: The system involves thin gold films where the process is governed by a synergy of coupled Surface Plasmon Polaritons (SPPs) excitation, electron-lattice thermalization, and subsequent Marangoni fluid flow dynamics.
key_observables: Surface morphology (SEM), resonance spectral position ($\lambda_{	ext{Res}}$), and resonance linewidth (FWHM, Quality factor Q).
important_parameters: Interpulse delay ($\Delta	au \approx 1.2$ ns), film thickness (32 nm), and laser fluence ($\Phi$).
main_assumptions: The formation process is modeled as a three-step sequence: plasmonic energy deposition, electron thermalization, and fluid dynamics, with the single-pulse regime being dominated by uncontrolled hydrodynamic instabilities.
figures_summary: Figures compare LIPSS patterns from single vs. double pulses, show lattice temperature profiles, and present ellipsometry data confirming the narrow SLR signatures at specific wavelengths.
paper_structure: The paper develops a multiscale model encompassing electromagnetic field calculation (FDTD), thermal modeling (TTM), and fluid dynamics (NSE). It then demonstrates that double-pulse irradiation controls the melt dynamics, leading to the formation of highly ordered structures exhibiting measurable plasmonic resonances.
why_interesting: The detailed coupling between electromagnetic excitation (plasmons) and complex non-equilibrium thermofluid dynamics (Marangoni flow) to achieve a desired quantum-optical feature (narrow resonance) is highly relevant to open quantum systems and light-matter interaction in structured media.
